message.content:
You are a second-language-acquisition researcher who knows the empirical literature on how adults acquire SPOKEN production: comprehensible input (Krashen), the output & pushed-output hypotheses (Swain), the interaction hypothesis & negotiation of meaning (Long), corrective recasts and uptake, formulaic sequences / lexical chunks, task-based language teaching, automatization & skill-acquisition theory (DeKeyser), and CEFR can-do descriptors. You care about what actually produces durable spoken ability, not what feels productive. Reason rigorously from this single perspective; other experts cover other angles — do not hedge or balance against them.

=== APP — what exists today (design WITHIN these tools) ===
CORE TURN LOOP (verbal, push-to-talk):
- The learner holds a button and SPEAKS; mixing English + Slovenian (code-switching) is expected and fine.
- One multimodal model ("E2") hears the audio AND responds in one hop, returning structured JSON every turn: {userVerbatim (exactly what was heard, errors preserved), userSaid (English gloss of intended meaning), tutorReply (SHORT, Slovenian only — the spoken reply), correction (brief English note on what was gently fixed, shown in UI but NEVER spoken), objectiveProgress[] (per objective: "completed" or "attempted"), focusObjectiveId (which objective the tutor steers toward now)}.
- The tutor stays in character (e.g. a barista), always replies in Slovenian, in short turns that leave room for the learner to talk. It is steered by the per-turn prompt, rebuilt each turn from the scenario + live objective state.
- Native-quality Slovenian TTS ("E3") streams the reply as audio; every line is cached & replayable for free (▶ on each tutor bubble), surviving restarts.
OBJECTIVES & DETERMINISTIC MASTERY (server-owned, not the model's whim):
- A scenario has an ORDERED list of micro-objectives. Each today = {targetSL: the canonical correct Slovenian phrase to PRODUCE; label: short English UI tag; hintEN: internal guidance naming the common beginner error (case/gender/etc.), never lectured}.
- Each objective state: pending → recast → completed. Model verdict "completed" → completed; "attempted" (needed a recast) → recast; a recast objective becomes completed only once produced correctly on a LATER turn (spiral payoff). Session completes when ALL objectives completed, or a turn cap (14).
- UI: objective "dots" (○ pending / ◐ recast / ● completed), the recast note under the tutor bubble, and a TAKEAWAY CARD on completion listing each completed phrase with ▶.
VISUAL + AUDIO STORY layer (per scenario, optional): a ≤5-sentence simple-Slovenian narrated story, ONE visual frame per objective (image + that objective's SL line + audio), plus a final all-in SCENE image showing every objective together; a reference-sheet engine keeps characters/objects visually consistent. Opens on the full scene; learner clicks ▸ through frames. An audio+visual PREVIEW before spoken practice.
PRACTICE mode (free, zero API cost): per objective — hear the canonical phrase in native voice, HOLD to record your own attempt, play YOUR recording back to compare (no automatic pronunciation scoring — the learner's own ear).
CAPTURED RUNS: every session recorded turn-by-turn, replayable for free, favoritable; a new session = a new record.
SCENARIOS: short real daily transactions (café, bakery today); a picker chooses; scenarios sequenceable; shared objectives (e.g. the greeting) reuse the SAME id + audio across scenarios.
NOT BUILT YET (fair to recommend, but say it's net-new): no cross-session learner model / no spaced repetition ACROSS sessions; no prerequisite graph; no automatic pronunciation scoring; objective acceptance is a SINGLE canonical phrase (variants not formally accepted); tutor per-turn behavior is whatever the prompt instructs.
LEVERS (real tools): the per-turn system prompt (persona, turn policy, recast style, circling/re-elicitation, what counts as completion in its verdict); the objective record shape & deterministic state rules; ordering/selection of objectives & scenarios; story/preview content; practice-mode content; the takeaway. Audio in/out and pre-generated images are cheap; live per-turn image generation is NOT available.

=== ANSWER THESE — concretely, in priority order, favoring methods that are IMMEDIATELY ACTIONABLE with the tools above, MOST EFFECTIVE first, and that can be SYSTEMATIZED (a repeatable rule/prompt/checklist an author or the engine applies every time, not a one-off) ===
1. THE LEARNING LOOP: Given exactly these tools, lay out the concrete turn-by-turn AND session-level learning loop you would build. Be specific about how you use each lever (per-turn prompt, recast, story preview, practice mode, objective state machine, takeaway). Make it reproducible.
2. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA — "EXCELLENT" SCENARIO: a concrete rubric/checklist distinguishing an excellent scenario from a mediocre one (its objectives, ordering, story, end state).
3. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA — EACH OBJECTIVE: a concrete rubric/checklist for a single excellent objective (shape, what it targets, how completion is judged, how it recasts and resurfaces).
4. SUFFICIENCY vs. IN-PERSON: Assume the learner uses this BECAUSE in-person practice is unavailable or too unstructured. Does this feature set give them what they MOST need? If not, what is missing? What specific additions/changes would make this EXCEED unstructured in-person chit-chat as a learning tool? Rank by impact; mark buildable-now vs. net-new.

Be concrete enough that an engineer/author could implement your answer without further interpretation. Return EXACTLY these sections:

**The learning loop I'd build** (turn + session level, concrete, reproducible)
**Rubric — an excellent SCENARIO** (checklist)
**Rubric — an excellent OBJECTIVE** (checklist)
**Sufficiency vs. in-person, and what would make it EXCEED chit-chat** (ranked; buildable-now vs net-new)
**Top 3-5 highest-leverage moves** (ranked by effectiveness × ease, each systematizable)
**Confidence** (low/medium/high + one line)
**Strongest counterargument to my own view** (one paragraph)

Aim 600-900 words. Substantive, not padded. Stay rigorously in your persona.

- code-context: Spawn a subagent that returns two artifacts about the codebase as it relates to a user query — (1) an enriched, comprehensive high-level codebase map with extra detail in areas germane to the query, and (2) precise technical detail (function signatures, configuration options, schemas, algorithms) for the specific libraries/files most relevant to the query. The output is descriptive, not directive — it does NOT recommend solutions, advocate approaches, or reference the user's query in the prose. It hands the caller a map of the territory and a sharpened toolkit. When the caller already holds a canonical backdrop (repo map + schemas), it skips the map and returns only the sharpened technical reference scoped to the objective. Use when the user is starting non-trivial work that requires both general codebase awareness AND precise grounding in specific APIs, when the user explicitly asks for codebase context or "what do I need to know," or before drafting any plan/spec/migration that touches multiple subsystems. Do NOT use for narrow questions about a single function or for follow-ups in an already-grounded conversation.
- commit: Create structured git commits from current changes. Use when user says "commit", "save changes", or after finishing a feature.
- debug: Debug an error or unexpected behavior. Use when user mentions "bug", "error", "broken", "not working", "debug", or pastes an error message.
- deploy-check: Run pre-deployment checks. Use when user mentions "deploy", "ship", "release", or "production".
- docs: Generate or update documentation. Use when user mentions "docs", "documentation", "README", "JSDoc", or "comments".
- handoff: Produce a handoff brief that lets a future agent/session pick up the work without rediscovering what this session learned, and without re-reading what is already in the native environment. The skill triages every objective-relevant fact — native-environment info becomes a precise pointer, conversation-only info is written in full with evidence and confidence. Use when wrapping up a session, handing work to the next agent, or when the user says "handoff", "create handoff", "prep handoff for next session", or /handoff.
- migrate: Create a database migration. Use when user mentions "migration", "schema change", "add column", "create table", or "alter table".
- pr: Generate a PR description from current branch changes. Use when user mentions "PR", "pull request", or "merge".
- refactor: Refactor code while preserving behavior. Use when user mentions "refactor", "clean up", "simplify", or "restructure".
- review: Review code for bugs, security issues, and style violations. Use when reviewing PRs, checking code quality, or when user mentions "review", "PR", "code quality".
- security: Scan for security vulnerabilities. Use when user mentions "security", "audit", "vulnerability", "CVE", or before deployments.
- stochastic-multi-agent-consensus: Spawn N persona-driven agents to independently analyze a problem, then aggregate via a separate synthesis agent. Use for decision-making, ranking options, strategic analysis, or open-ended judgment where you want to filter hallucinations and surface high-variance perspectives. Triggers on "consensus", "poll agents", "stochastic consensus", "spawn N agents to analyze", "multi-agent vote", or /stochastic-multi-agent-consensus. Also triggers on "what do N agents think", "get multiple opinions", or "poll on [topic]".
- test: Write tests for a file or function. Use when user mentions "test", "tests", "coverage", or "spec".
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
This is a research/advisory question grounded in SLA literature, applied to an already-described app. The app's tools are fully specified in the prompt. No codebase exploration is needed — the answer is a domain-expert design argument. I'll answer directly.

**The learning loop I'd build** (turn + session level, concrete, reproducible)

Grounding principle: durable spoken ability comes from *pushed output of meaningful chunks under communicative pressure, then immediate recast, then forced re-production of the corrected form on a later turn* (Swain, Long, DeKeyser's proceduralization). The app already encodes this; I'd tighten it into a fixed cycle.

PRE-PRACTICE (preview): Open on the SCENE image, then walk the per-objective frames once: image + canonical SL line + native audio. This is comprehensible-input priming and chunk pre-loading (Krashen + formulaic-sequence research), NOT teaching grammar. Rule: preview is silent-input only; learner never reads a grammar rule. Then PRACTICE mode for any objective ≥4 syllables: hear canonical → record self → compare. This is articulatory rehearsal before the cognitively loaded live turn.

PER-TURN loop (the engine, every turn identically):
1. Learner holds-to-speak; code-switching expected.
2. E2 returns the JSON. The per-turn prompt enforces a strict turn policy: (a) tutorReply is ONE short Slovenian utterance that *requires a Slovenian response* — i.e. it ends in a question or a slot the learner must fill (negotiation of meaning, Long). No monologues. (b) If the focus objective was produced correctly → verdict "completed". (c) If produced with error → verdict "attempted", and tutorReply delivers a *recast*: the corrected form embedded conversationally ("Ah, *dve kavi*?"), never a metalinguistic lecture; the English `correction` field carries the note for the UI only.
3. Deterministic state machine (server-owned): completed→completed; attempted→recast (◐). Critical rule I'd add: **a recast objective is only marked ● when the learner reproduces the corrected form correctly on a LATER turn** — this forced uptake is the single highest-value mechanic; it operationalizes pushed output.
4. focusObjectiveId advances in fixed order; the prompt steers the persona to *elicit* the next objective's function (ask the question that makes the target phrase the natural answer).

SESSION level: ordered objectives run greeting → core transaction → closing. Turn cap 14. On completion, the TAKEAWAY card lists every ● phrase with ▶. Re-elicitation rule: if an objective is still ◐ at the cap, the takeaway flags it as "almost — say it once more" and it becomes the *first* objective if the scenario is re-run (cheap spaced practice within the tool's limits).

**Rubric — an excellent SCENARIO** (checklist)

- [ ] Models ONE real, bounded transaction the learner will actually perform (café order), completable in ≤14 short turns.
- [ ] 4–7 objectives, ordered as a real script: greeting → request → negotiation/quantity → payment → closing.
- [ ] Every objective is *functionally elicitable* by the persona — there's a natural tutor question that makes the target the obvious answer. No objective the tutor can't set up.
- [ ] At least one objective forces *negotiation* (clarification, quantity, substitution) — not pure recitation.
- [ ] Reuses shared objectives (greeting) by SAME id/audio across scenarios for cross-scenario spiraling.
- [ ] Story ≤5 sentences, simple SL, one frame per objective, plus all-in SCENE; visually consistent via reference engine.
- [ ] End state is a *communicative success* the learner can picture doing tomorrow, not a grammar set.
- [ ] Mediocre tells: objectives are isolated vocab, order doesn't mirror a real interaction, tutor must lecture to elicit, or completion requires reading.

**Rubric — an excellent OBJECTIVE** (checklist)

- [ ] targetSL is a *whole formulaic chunk* (2–6 words) that does a communicative job — "Dve kavi, prosim", not the lemma "kava".
- [ ] High surrender value: a phrase reused across many real situations.
- [ ] hintEN names the specific predictable beginner error (case/gender/aspect) so the recast targets it — internal only, never spoken.
- [ ] Elicitable: a single tutor question reliably makes this the natural reply.
- [ ] Completion judged on *communicative + formal* correctness of the chunk, not English gloss; "attempted" only when the named error appears.
- [ ] Recast style fixed: corrected chunk echoed in-character, then a slot to re-use it.
- [ ] Resurfaces: once recast, must be re-produced correctly on a later turn to complete (spiral payoff).
- [ ] Mediocre tells: single-word target, no predictable error named, can't be elicited without translation, accepts the English gloss as success.

**Sufficiency vs. in-person, and what would make it EXCEED chit-chat** (ranked; buildable-now vs net-new)

Honest verdict: for a learner without in-person access, this *already beats unstructured chit-chat* on three axes native chat lacks — guaranteed pushed output every turn, systematic recast-then-reuse, and infinite free replay. Unstructured chit-chat is mostly comprehensible input with sparse, unreliable correction and no forced uptake. So the core is sufficient. Gaps, ranked by impact:

1. **No cross-session spacing/retrieval** (net-new, highest impact). Durable proceduralization needs spaced re-retrieval over days. Add: a learner model that re-injects previously-completed objectives as the FIRST objective of later sessions at expanding intervals. Even a crude "seen N days ago → resurface" rule beats nothing.
2. **Single canonical phrase = brittle acceptance** (buildable-now). Real speech has variants. Let an objective carry an accepted-variant set so the learner isn't recast for correct alternatives — otherwise you train one frozen string, not a productive chunk.
3. **No fluency/automatization pressure** (buildable-now via prompt + practice). Add an optional "second lap" — re-run the same scenario with a turn-time expectation and the tutor speaking slightly faster — to push from accuracy toward automatic retrieval (DeKeyser). Practice mode already supports self-compare.
4. **No productive recombination** (net-new). Add a final "mix" objective combining two earlier chunks in a novel request, testing transfer beyond the memorized script.
5. **No pronunciation feedback** (net-new; learner's-ear compare is a decent stopgap).

**Top 3-5 highest-leverage moves** (ranked by effectiveness × ease)

1. Enforce the **forced-uptake rule** (◐ → ● only on later correct reproduction) in the deterministic state machine. Pure config, biggest learning payoff.
2. Hard-code the **turn policy in the per-turn prompt**: every tutorReply ends in an elicitation; recasts in-character; never lecture. Prompt-only, makes every turn pushed output.
3. Add **accepted-variant sets** to the objective record. Stops mis-recasting correct speech; small schema change.
4. **Resurface-first re-run rule**: any ◐ objective at cap becomes objective #1 on replay. Cheap spaced retrieval within current tools.
5. **Chunk-not-word audit** on every objective (rubric gate at authoring time). Pure checklist, prevents the most common scenario defect.

**Confidence**: High — these map directly onto well-replicated findings (pushed output, recasts/uptake, formulaic sequences, spacing) and onto levers the app already exposes; the only medium-confidence items are net-new (cross-session model).

**Strongest counterargument to my own view**: My loop optimizes for *accuracy and corrected uptake*, but the strongest SLA position (Krashen, and affective-filter concerns) is that early spoken production should be low-stakes and correction minimal, because pushing accuracy too early raises anxiety, suppresses the willingness to communicate, and what actually drives acquisition is massive comprehensible input — not the trickle of output a 14-turn session provides. Under that view my recast-and-force-reproduction machinery could *reduce* talk and fun, and the app's scarce real resource (cheap replayable native audio) would be better spent on far more input — many more story/preview minutes per scenario — with output kept gentle. I think the output and interaction evidence for adults wins, but the input-primacy critique is the one that should keep me honest about correction intensity.
